extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers, bankers, and merchants
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, criteria, and analytical distinctions about paper money, banking practice, and the distinction between productive and unproductive labour; aimed at informing monetary policy and the management/accumulation of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum denomination for bank notes
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be better that no bank notes were issued in any part of the kingdom for a smaller sum than £5; in London no bank notes under £10 are issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-denomination notes extend paper money into transactions with consumers and tend to displace gold and silver; suppressing ten and five shilling notes in Scotland relieved scarcity of gold and silver. Example: London confines notes to higher denominations which keeps metal currency plentiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine paper money to circulation between dealers
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper money should be pretty much confined to the circulation between dealers and dealers rather than between dealers and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When paper is mainly used among dealers (as in London), gold and silver remain abundant; when it extends to consumer transactions (as in Scotland and North America), it banishes metals almost entirely from interior commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convertibility and unconditional payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper money issued by people of undoubted credit, payable upon demand, without condition, and readily paid when presented is equal in value to gold and silver money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such notes command the same purchasing power because gold/silver can always be had for them; therefore goods bought with such paper should be no dearer than for coin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper dependent on issuer goodwill or deferred payment is inferior
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper money consisting of promissory notes whose immediate payment depends on the issuer's goodwill, or is payable only at a future date and bears no interest, will fall below the value of gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The greater the uncertainty or distant the term of payment, the more the paper will be discounted relative to coin; example: North American colonial paper payable many years hence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional deferred-payment clauses degrade bank notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting an optional clause permitting directors to defer payment (e.g., six months) degrades the notes below the value of gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scotland's optional-clause practice (directors threatening to invoke six-month option) led to notes trading at several percent discount (example: 4% against gold in Dumfries vs Carlisle). Suppressing such clauses restored natural exchange rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clauses making small-change conditional are unlawful and deleterious
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions that make payment of small denominations dependent on the holder fulfilling inconvenient conditions (e.g., bringing change) degrade the currency and have been declared unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Yorkshire notes of 6d requiring the bearer to bring change of a guinea—such conditions make the notes less valuable than coin and were suppressed by act of parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government long-term paper as legal tender unjust to creditors
rubrics_metrics.description: A government paper whose payment is not exigible till several years after issue (and which pays no interest) — made legal tender — unjustly forces creditors to accept a nominal sum worth far less in ready money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: colonial emissions where £100 payable in 15 years was worth only ~£40 in ready money (at 6%); forcing creditors to accept such paper was 'violent injustice' and appears as debtor fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal tender cannot compel market pricing equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive law can make a tender discharge a debt (legal tender), but it cannot compel a seller freely selling goods to accept a depreciated paper as equivalent in price to gold and silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalizing price differentials (selling for paper vs coin at different prices) is tyrannical and largely ineffectual; market exchange rates reveal true relative value despite legal fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper used to pay taxes gains additional value
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper of a colony that is receivable in payment of provincial taxes derives additional value above what it would otherwise have, because a portion of demand is created by the need to pay taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This additional value depends on how much paper is issued relative to what can be employed in paying taxes; if kept below that quantity it may even bear a premium (bank of Amsterdam example), though that account may be exaggerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of paper money does not necessarily change total currency quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: When paper is added to the currency, the quantity of gold and silver taken from the currency is always equal to the paper added, so paper does not necessarily increase the whole currency quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price movements attributed to increase in paper hinge on the net effect on total currency (metal + paper) and on metal supplies from mines; historical examples show no necessary correlation between more paper and higher provisions' prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of small notes can restore metal abundance and exchange parity
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppressing small-denomination notes and optional clauses can relieve scarcity of coin and restore natural exchange between regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: suppression of 10s and 5s in Scotland relieved gold/silver scarcity; same act suppressed optional clauses and restored exchange rates between England and Scotland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bankers: restrict small-note issuance and require immediate payment for safety
rubrics_metrics.description: If bankers are restrained from issuing circulating notes below a certain sum and are obliged to immediate and unconditional payment of notes when presented, their trade can otherwise be perfectly free and safe for the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such restrictions reduce runs and misbehaviour; competition among many banking companies increases security by making each more circumspect and dividing circulation so individual failures are less consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of banking companies increases public security
rubrics_metrics.description: The late multiplication of banking companies, instead of diminishing, increases public security by forcing circumspection, limiting each company's currency relative to cash, and dividing overall circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More competitors restrain any one bank from overextending; free competition makes bankers more liberal to customers and reduces risk from any single failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper currency value depends on quantity emitted and redemption term
rubrics_metrics.description: The market value of a colony's paper relative to sterling depends on how much paper is emitted and the distance/probability of its final discharge and redemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: colonial paper sometimes valued at £130 or £1100 currency to £100 sterling depending on emission quantities and redemption terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of productive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Productive labour is that which adds to the value of the subject upon which it is bestowed and fixes or realizes itself in a vendible commodity that endures after the labour is past; it effectively 'stocks' labour into a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: manufacturer's labour adds value to materials and is restored in wages and profit; the improved subject can later set other labour in motion equivalent to what produced it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unproductive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Unproductive labour adds to nothing that endures; its services generally perish at the moment of performance and leave no trace of value for which an equal quantity of service could later be procured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: menial servants, sovereign and officers of justice/war, actors, musicians, many men of letters — their work does not produce vendible commodities that replace capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official/domestic services classified as unproductive despite usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereign, officers of justice and war, the army and navy, and some respectable professions (churchmen, lawyers, physicians) are unproductive labourers in the sense that their services do not realize in durable vendible commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their maintenance comes from the annual produce of others; usefulness, honour, or necessity does not make labour productive unless it yields a vendible durable value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual produce divides into capital replacement and revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual produce naturally divides into (1) a part destined for replacing capital (renewing provisions, materials, finished work) and (2) a part constituting revenue (profit or rent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The capital-replacement part typically pays wages of productive labour only; the revenue part can maintain either productive or unproductive hands and constitutes owners' incomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital replacement funds maintain productive hands only
rubrics_metrics.description: That part of annual produce which replaces capital is employed to maintain productive hands only and is not immediately directed to maintaining unproductive hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only after productive labour has been put in motion and capital's function fulfilled can any surplus be used to maintain unproductive hands; workmen must earn wages before spending on unproductive consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue maintains unproductive or productive hands; proportion matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenue (rent or profits) may maintain either productive or unproductive hands; the relative sizes of funds destined for capital replacement vs revenue determine the proportion of productive to unproductive labour in a country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rich countries a larger proportion of produce replaces capital (favoring productive labour); in poor or feudal systems more goes to revenue (favoring unproductive maintenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony (saving) increases capital; industry alone does not
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals are increased by parsimony (saving from revenue) and diminished by prodigality; industry provides the subject which parsimony accumulates, but saving is the immediate cause of capital growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What a person saves from revenue is added to capital and employed to maintain additional productive hands or lent at interest; society's capital increases only through aggregate saving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of capital to revenue determines industry vs idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever capital predominates, industry prevails; wherever revenue predominates, idleness prevails. Changes in capital thus alter the number of productive hands and the real wealth of inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mercantile/manufacturing towns (capital-dominated) show industriousness and prosperity; court-residence towns (revenue-dominated) show idleness and poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saved portion of revenue supports productive employment indirectly
rubrics_metrics.description: What is annually saved is consumed in due course like what is spent, but by a different set of people: savings (parsimony) put into capital support productive employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consumption arising from saved revenues funds productive labourers (via investment/lending), whereas spent revenue often sustains unproductive consumption (guests, servants).
